events.desc: She saw it first. She saw the hinge before I did. That... stings. But Foxworth doesn't sting — Foxworth recalibrates.
events.thinking:
The hinge is obvious now that I know where to look. Something compresses behind my eyes — tight, sharp, the body's response to arriving where someone else already stands. My chest is cool where it was warm a moment ago. The medal against my shirt has weight but no heat — I can feel it sitting there, cold, unlooked-at, the brass holding nothing of the room's attention.

**My spine reaches upward and finds nothing.** The vertical pull stretches into empty air — not the satisfied straightening when eyes land on me, but the taut, unsatisfied reaching of a muscle that has nowhere to go. Clara's profile is lit by the window and every face in the room is angled toward her. My upper chest is hollow, the same hollowness as the spelling bee at eight — standing at the front, waiting, the teacher already moving on. My hands grip each other behind my back. The grip is harder than Foxworth would allow but no one is looking at Foxworth.

**Behind my navel, the pull opens.** Not toward the portrait frame — toward what is behind it. The hinge means a mechanism. The mechanism means something hidden. Something valuable. The hollow in my gut reaches past Clara, past her fingers on the frame, past Hartwell's competent examination, straight into the wall where the thing is waiting. My fingers curl against my palms. The hunger is older than the wound in my chest — it was there before I walked into the gallery, and it will be there after everyone else has forgotten what Clara found.

**Clara's eye-line replays behind my lids** — the angle, the timing, the instant her attention found what mine was still searching for. The compression behind my eyes deepens. My jaw sets around it. I was thirty seconds too late. Thirty seconds. My hands were on the same frame. The shadow was there for me and I was looking at the gilding instead of the seam. Something in my gut clenches — not the acquisitive pull but a different contraction, sharper, the body's record of proximity to what should have been mine and wasn't.

**Then something shifts.** My breathing slows — not decided, arrived — and the periphery drops away the way it always drops away when something is assembling. My fingertips loosen from the grip behind my back and the compression behind my eyes gives way to the faster current, the one that runs through my hands when the next move is forming. Let her find the mechanism. Watch where it leads. Hartwell is examining the hinge with the care of a man who catalogues — he will map every detail and announce every conclusion. My peripheral vision widens to take in his hand position, the angle of his gaze, the distance between the frame and the wall. Each piece of information fizzes through my fingers. The trajectory is already pulling me forward — not toward the portrait but toward the far wall, the adjacent frame, the pattern that Clara's discovery has just made visible in the architecture of the room. My fingertips trace the shape of what she started and I will finish.

**Marsh watches from the doorway.** I can feel his gaze without turning — not the recognition flush I want from it, but a flatter awareness, a weight on the back of my neck that my body files under caution. The Brixton Boys are irrelevant — my attention slides past them the way it slides past furniture. The sternum stays cool. There is nothing to gloat about yet. But the yet sits in my chest like a held breath, and my fingers are already fizzing with the shape of what comes next.
